sense: rest one’s weight against or on something

terms.gloss: lean or rest on, support oneself on
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, deponent, with the ablative or the dative
terms.comment: The prose word for resting one’s weight on a support: a stick, a spear, a column, someone’s arm (in Pansam frātrem innīxus, Plin. NH 7.182, Lewis & Short). Figuratively, to rely on. For pushing against something with the feet, see lean on.

terms.grammar: adjective, third declension, with the dative
terms.register: vōx plērumque poētica: Verg., Ov.; in ōrātiōne solūtā post Augustum
evidence: Verg. A. 10.834: arboris acclīnis truncō (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: bend, lean (the body, a thing) to one side
terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, transitive; also intransitive, or with sē
evidence: Lucr. 2.243: paulum inclīnāre necesse est corpora (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: in the literal sense mostly poetic and post-Augustan; Cicero uses it figuratively, of opinion and fortune turning one way (sē ad Stōicōs inclīnāre, Fin. 3.10).

phrases.english: and he was easing his body, leaning against the trunk of a tree

phrases.latin: Nōlī mūrō innītī: tectōrium nōndum siccum est.
phrases.english: Don’t lean on the wall: the plaster isn’t dry yet.
Grandpa walks leaning on a stick.

sources: Lewis & Short: innitor · Lewis & Short: acclinis · Lewis & Short: inclino
